outages.title: CrowdStrike faulty update
outages.scale: 8.5 million Windows devices; 125 Fortune 500 corporations affected
outages.loss_detail: $5.4B direct loss to US Fortune 500 excluding Microsoft. Weighted average $44M per affected company. Healthcare worst hit at $1.938B.
outages.retail_impact: 43% of retailers and wholesalers in the Fortune 500 cohort suffered direct costs
outages.relevance: Point-of-sale and back-office systems froze. A local balancer with no cloud dependency keeps in-store transaction routing alive.
outages.source: Parametrix Insurance, CrowdStrike's Impact on the Fortune 500

outages.title: Rogers nationwide network outage
outages.scale: 12+ million subscribers; 15 hours to several days
outages.loss_detail: Interac debit went offline nationwide. Businesses could not accept debit payments regardless of their own ISP. Some stores closed for the day. 9-1-1 calls failed in multiple cities.
outages.relevance: The strongest argument in this deck: the merchants who went down had working local networks and working local hardware. Only the upstream path failed. Local-first routing is the mitigation, and Interac's own remediation was exactly that - a secondary carrier plus a third backup link, completed June 2023.
outages.source: CBC News; Interac Corp. statement; Wikipedia, 2022 Rogers Communications outage

downtime_costs.metric: Unscheduled downtime cost to the world's 500 largest companies
downtime_costs.detail: $1.4 trillion per year, equal to 11% of annual revenues, up from $864B (8%) in 2019-20. Automotive: $2.3M per hour. Average large plant loses 27 hours per month.

downtime_costs.source: Aberdeen Group, cited in Siemens True Cost of Downtime analysis

downtime_costs.detail: Average across SMBs; most experience multiple downtime events per year. We use this figure rather than the far higher ITIC estimates because it is the conservative one and our scenarios are small-business scale.
downtime_costs.source: Datto, State of the Channel Ransomware Report 2023
downtime_costs.caveat: ITIC 2024 reports much higher self-reported figures, over $100K/hr even for micro-SMBs. Those are respondent estimates skewed toward IT-dependent firms. We deliberately present the conservative $8,000 number so the savings case cannot be attacked as inflated.

academic.claim: Reinforcement learning cuts total execution delay substantially versus classical multi-criteria scheduling in fog networks
academic.figures: 82% improvement at high task-generation rates, 87% at medium, 90% at the lowest, for Double Deep Q-Learning versus ELECTRE
academic.source: Privacy-Aware Load Balancing in Fog Networks: A Reinforcement Learning Approach

academic.claim: Q-learning applied to multi-controller load balancing in SDN reduces latency and improves throughput
academic.source: Artificial intelligence based load balancing in SDN: A comprehensive survey

academic.claim: Honest counter-evidence: Q-learning schedulers can trade raw response time for fairness
academic.figures: Expected response time increased by up to 14% while fairness improved 12-27% versus OLB, MET, MCT and k-Percent Best
academic.source: Q-Learning Scheduler and Load Balancer for Heterogeneous Systems
academic.why_included: Including a paper that contradicts the easy story is what separates a research claim from a sales pitch. Address it directly in the viva: our reward function targets latency explicitly, which is why we do not see this trade-off.

academic.claim: RL-based dynamic load balancing is an active research direction in edge computing networks
academic.source: Reinforcement learning-based dynamic load balancing in edge computing networks, Computer Communications (2024)

novelty_claims._note: What we actually claim as novel. Keep these narrow and defensible - an overbroad claim is the fastest way to lose a viva.

claims.claim: On-device reinforcement learning for L7 traffic distribution on a sub-$5 microcontroller, with no cloud, no coordinator, and no pre-training phase.
claims.defensible_because: Published RL load balancing work targets cloud, SDN controllers or fog nodes, all of which assume at minimum a Linux-class host. We run the Bellman update in 520 KB of RAM on bare metal.

claims.claim: The Q-table is state-aware on concurrency, not just server identity: state is the number of active proxy sessions, action is the backend choice.
claims.defensible_because: A bare bandit approach, which EMA effectively is, ignores load context. Our formulation learns that the right backend at 1 concurrent session differs from the right backend at 6.

claims.claim: Learning happens online, in production traffic, from a reward derived from real observed session duration - not from a simulator.
claims.defensible_because: No offline training dataset, no model upload. The device is useful from the first request and improves without intervention.

claims.claim: Total system cost and power are low enough that N+1 redundancy is economically free.
claims.defensible_because: Three ESP32 units cost less than a tenth of one Raspberry Pi and draw less power combined than one Pi at idle. Redundancy that costs nothing gets deployed; redundancy that costs money does not.

honest_limitations: Hard ceiling of 7 concurrent proxy sessions. The ESP32 has 16 sockets, 1 for the listener and 2 per session. This is a real architectural limit, not a tuning issue.
No TLS termination. The ESP32 can do TLS but not at meaningful throughput while also proxying.
The Q-table is lost on reboot, not yet persisted to NVS. Relearning takes a few dozen requests.
Suited to low-request-rate, high-value traffic such as POS terminals, sensor gateways and kiosks - not to general web serving.

scenarios.name: Smart Factory Sensor Gateway
scenarios.tagline: When a processing node stalls, the queue backs up in seconds
scenarios.setting: A mid-size component manufacturer runs 48 vibration and temperature sensors on the shop floor, feeding three local edge processing nodes that run anomaly detection. The nodes sit in a control cabinet. There is no cloud link on the production VLAN, by policy.
scenarios.problem: Node 2 shares a cabinet with a variable-frequency drive and thermally throttles during the afternoon shift. Its processing latency climbs from 40 ms to 900 ms. A round-robin distributor keeps feeding it one third of all sensor traffic. Analysis queues back up, anomaly alerts arrive late, and a bearing failure is caught 40 minutes later than it should have been.
scenarios.why_esp32: The cabinet has no spare mains outlet and no room for a fanned device. An ESP32 runs off the existing 24 V DIN-rail supply through a buck converter, has no fan to clog with metal dust, and has no SD card to corrupt when the line is E-stopped.
scenarios.what_to_watch: Round Robin keeps hammering the degraded node at a fixed 33%. Q-learning detects the reward collapse and drains it within a few dozen requests, without ever being told which node is sick.

economic_anchor.framing: We do not claim to save $260,000 per hour. We claim that catching a degrading node 40 minutes earlier is worth a meaningful fraction of one hour of line stoppage, against a hardware cost of under $15.

events.label: Cabinet fan kicks in, Node 2 recovers

scenarios.name: Rural Clinic Telemedicine Kiosk
scenarios.tagline: Solar budget, intermittent uplink, no IT staff
scenarios.setting: A primary health centre serving 11 villages runs four patient-intake kiosks and a teleconsultation terminal. Power comes from a 400 W solar array with a 12 V battery bank. The satellite uplink is available roughly 60% of the working day. Patient records are served from two local mini-servers so that intake never blocks on the uplink.
scenarios.problem: Every watt drawn by infrastructure is a watt not available for the vaccine refrigerator. A Raspberry Pi acting as gateway draws 2.7 W idle and 6.4 W under load. Running 24/7 that is meaningful against a battery bank sized for medical equipment. Worse, hard power cuts during monsoon corrupt the Pi's SD card every few months, and there is no one on site to reflash it.
scenarios.why_esp32: Sub-watt draw, cold boot in about a second after a power cut, and nothing to corrupt. When the battery dips, the balancer is the last thing you have to worry about.
scenarios.what_to_watch: Server B is an older machine that slows badly under concurrent intake. Watch the power meter alongside the latency chart. The ESP32's annual energy cost is a rounding error against a Pi's, and against a mini-PC's it is not close.

economic_anchor.metric: Annual energy cost and 5-year TCO for the gateway device
economic_anchor.framing: Computed live in the simulation from the power figures. The headline is not the money, it is that the power budget is what makes the deployment possible at all.

events.label: Server B bogs down under concurrent intake
Server A load rises as traffic shifts to it

scenarios.name: Retail POS During a Cloud Outage
scenarios.tagline: The day the cloud went down and the shop stayed open
scenarios.setting: A five-outlet restaurant chain runs six point-of-sale terminals and two kitchen display screens per outlet. Order routing normally goes through a cloud POS backend. Two local mini-servers hold a full offline mirror of the menu, pricing and order queue.
scenarios.problem: On 19 July 2024 the CrowdStrike update took down 8.5 million Windows machines, and 43% of Fortune 500 retailers and wholesalers took direct costs. On 8 July 2022 the Rogers outage took Interac debit offline nationwide - merchants could not take debit payments even though their own ISP was fine. In both cases the local network and local hardware were healthy. Only the path upward failed.
scenarios.why_esp32: The balancer has no cloud dependency, no upstream heartbeat, and no license check. If the LAN is up, order routing is up. At $4 per unit, every outlet can keep a cold spare in a drawer.
scenarios.what_to_watch: At tick 60 the WAN link drops entirely. A cloud-dependent setup flatlines - that is the grey line going to zero. The ESP32 path keeps serving from the local mirrors throughout, and Q-learning rebalances when one mirror gets overwhelmed by the redirected load.

economic_anchor.framing: Conservative figure, deliberately chosen. A 15-hour outage of the Rogers kind at $8,000 per hour is $120,000, against a hardware cost of roughly $12 for three units.

simulation_findings._note: Results produced by the simulation engine (ui/static/sim-engine.js), which is a line-for-line port of the firmware algorithms. Reproduce with: node benchmarks/tools/verify_sim.mjs and the exp_*.mjs experiments. These are SIMULATED results and are labelled as such wherever they appear in the deck. They are not a substitute for the hardware benchmark.

primary_metric.name: Goodput
primary_metric.definition: Share of all offered requests that received a real answer. Counts timeouts AND 503 rejections as failures.
primary_metric.why: Mean latency alone is survivorship-biased. A strategy that lets sessions occupy all 7 ESP32 sockets until new arrivals are refused posts a flattering average precisely because the slow requests were never served. From the client's point of view a 503 and a timeout are the same event: no answer. Goodput is the metric that cannot be gamed this way, and adopting it changed our conclusions - under mean latency Round Robin looked competitive in the factory scenario; under goodput it loses by 15 points.

headline_finding.claim: Q-learning's advantage is conditional on backend heterogeneity, and we have quantified the threshold.
headline_finding.detail: With two backends and six clients, holding everything else constant and sweeping only the latency spread between them, averaged over 8 seeds.
headline_finding.interpretation: Below roughly 5x spread every strategy saturates - the backends are interchangeable, so the routing decision does not matter and Round Robin is the correct engineering choice because it is free. Past 8x the picture inverts sharply: Round Robin collapses to 71% and then 50% goodput because it keeps sending a fixed share of traffic into a backend that cannot absorb it, while Q-learning holds 99% and 94%. This is the honest version of our claim - not 'RL is better', but 'RL earns its complexity exactly when backends diverge, and here is the measured threshold.'

known_weakness.title: Non-stationarity and the exploration floor
known_weakness.finding: In the retail scenario Q-learning UNDERPERFORMS Round Robin on goodput (74.5% vs 84.5%, mean of 8 seeds).
known_weakness.root_cause: Two things compound. First, epsilon decays from 1.0 to its 0.05 floor in 59 feedback updates; in the retail timeline that happens at roughly tick 40, about 74 updates BEFORE the backend degrades at tick 75. The agent is fully greedy before the world changes, and a 5% exploration rate is slow to discover it. Second, the two retail mirrors start nearly identical (55ms vs 60ms, a 1.09x spread), which by our own heterogeneity result is the regime where there is no signal to learn - so the argmax latches onto one mirror and self-reinforces, concentrating load instead of spreading it.
known_weakness.evidence: Raising min_epsilon from 0.05 to 0.15 lifts retail mean goodput from 74.5% to 85.5% across 8 seeds. Worst-seed goodput stays near 75%, so the exploration floor is a partial fix, not a cure.
known_weakness.we_did_not_hide_this: This weakness is presented in the deck on its own slide. A load balancer that is only tested where it wins has not been tested.
future_work: Epsilon resurgence: when observed reward falls far below the Q-value that predicted it, the policy is stale - temporarily raise epsilon to re-explore. Prototyped and measured: +8.4 points on retail but -1.8 on factory, mean +2.2. Not a clear enough win to justify changing shipped firmware, which is why it is future work and not a result.
Detect the low-heterogeneity regime at runtime (variance of the reward across backends) and fall back to Round Robin, which is provably optimal when backends are interchangeable.
Persist the Q-table to NVS so a reboot does not discard what was learned.
